cues.text: During Holy Mass on March 25, 1907, the Feast of the Annunciation, Father Fernando Gomez served as pastor of the Church of Our Lady of the Angels in Silla, Spain.
He went to the tabernacle to bring out the Hosts for Communion, but found its door already standing open, with the silver ciborium and its consecrated Hosts gone.
Two days later, the missing Hosts were found in a small garden on the outskirts of the city, concealed beneath a rock where the thief, or thieves, had apparently left them.
Father Gomez carried them back to the church in a solemn procession, and the parishioners themselves provided a sacred vessel to protect the recovered Hosts going forward.

In 1934, the Hosts were formally examined and found, in the words of the resulting report, to remain "in the same state in which they were recovered under the rock and maintained their original condition unaltered."
The Archbishop of Valencia began the process of declaring their preservation miraculous.
He had the reliquary containing them sealed with wax, along with a detailed written account of the case.

Two years later, in 1936, the Archbishop's palace was burned down amid the anticlerical violence of the Spanish Civil War, and the formal documentation of the case was lost in the fire along with much else.
It was not until 1982, on the 75th anniversary of the original theft, that Archbishop Miguel Roca of Valencia undertook a new canonical process and formally authorized public veneration of the Hosts.

The Hosts remain today in the tabernacle of the Church of Our Lady of the Angels in Silla, placed in a new reliquary for veneration on the tradition's centenary in 2007 and carried in procession to mark the occasion.
Like the earlier Onil tradition from the same region of Spain, Silla's account rests less on any single dramatic event.
Instead, it rests on simple, sustained physical preservation: a theft, a recovery, and then more than a century of a relic that has never shown the decay bread of its kind would ordinarily undergo.
